claim: Septins are guanine nucleotide-binding proteins that polymerize into filamentous and higher-order structures.
source: Septins are guanine nucleotide-binding proteins that polymerize into filamentous and higher-order structures.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the basic biochemical property of septins, supported by the broader scientific literature and the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Cdc42 and its effector Gic1 are involved in septin recruitment, ring formation and dissociation.
source: Cdc42 and its effector Gic1 are involved in septin recruitment, ring formation and dissociation.
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gic1 acts as a scaffolding protein for septin filaments forming long and flexible filament cables.
source: We show that Gic1 acts as a scaffolding protein for septin filaments forming long and flexible filament cables.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy and cryo-ET data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Cdc42 in its GTP-form binds to Gic1, which ultimately leads to the dissociation of Gic1 from the filament cables.
source: Cdc42 in its GTP-form binds to Gic1, which ultimately leads to the dissociation of Gic1 from the filament cables.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 5, 6, and 7 showing binding and dissociation.

claim: Cdc42-GDP directly interacts with septin filaments resulting in their disassembly in the absence of Gic1.
source: Surprisingly, Cdc42-GDP is not inactive, but in the absence of Gic1 directly interacts with septin filaments resulting in their disassembly.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Septins have been implicated in cytokinesis, spindle positioning, morphogenesis, and exocytosis.
source: Septins are ubiquitous guanine nucleotide-binding proteins that have been implicated in many cellular processes such as cytokinesis, spindle positioning, morphogenesis, and exocytosis, and their mutation or overexpression is associated with neoplasia, neurodegenerative diseases and male infertility (Hall and Russell, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hall and Russell, 2004.

claim: Mutation or overexpression of septins is associated with neoplasia, neurodegenerative diseases and male infertility.
source: Septins are ubiquitous guanine nucleotide-binding proteins that have been implicated in many cellular processes such as cytokinesis, spindle positioning, morphogenesis, and exocytosis, and their mutation or overexpression is associated with neoplasia, neurodegenerative diseases and male infertility (Hall and Russell, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hall and Russell, 2004.

claim: In yeast, four essential septins (Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11 and Cdc12) are found at the bud neck.
source: In yeast, four essential septins (Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11 and Cdc12) are found at the bud neck (Haarer and Pringle, 1987; Ford and Pringle, 1991; Kim et al., 1991), where they form an ordered ring composed of membrane-adjacent filaments (Hartwell, 1971; Byers and Goetsch, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Septins form an ordered ring composed of membrane-adjacent filaments at the bud neck.
source: In yeast, four essential septins (Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11 and Cdc12) are found at the bud neck (Haarer and Pringle, 1987; Ford and Pringle, 1991; Kim et al., 1991), where they form an ordered ring composed of membrane-adjacent filaments (Hartwell, 1971; Byers and Goetsch, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hartwell, 1971 and Byers and Goetsch, 1976.

claim: Seven different septins were identified in S. cerevisiae.
source: In total seven different septins were identified in S. cerevisiae, where they form filaments of variable size and combinations.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast septins.

claim: The human genome encodes thirteen septins.
source: Whereas the human genome encodes thirteen septins, C. elegans has only two and plants are devoid of septin genes (Hall and Russell, 2004; Ihara et al., 2005; Kinoshita, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall and Russell, 2004; Ihara et al., 2005; Kinoshita, 2006.

claim: C. elegans has only two septins.
source: Whereas the human genome encodes thirteen septins, C. elegans has only two and plants are devoid of septin genes (Hall and Russell, 2004; Ihara et al., 2005; Kinoshita, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall and Russell, 2004; Ihara et al., 2005; Kinoshita, 2006.

claim: Plants are devoid of septin genes.
source: Whereas the human genome encodes thirteen septins, C. elegans has only two and plants are devoid of septin genes (Hall and Russell, 2004; Ihara et al., 2005; Kinoshita, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall and Russell, 2004; Ihara et al., 2005; Kinoshita, 2006.

claim: All septins share defined structural features.
source: Despite the genetic variability, all septins share defined structural features.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about septin structure.

claim: Septins interact via their central guanine nucleotide-binding domains (G-domains) and/or the N- and C-terminal extensions forming oligomers and non-helical filaments.
source: Septins interact via their central guanine nucleotide-binding domains (G-domains) and/or the N- and C-terminal extensions forming oligomers and non-helical filaments.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic study cited (Sirajuddin et al., 2007, 2009) and represents established structural knowledge.

claim: The basic structural unit of the yeast septin complex is an octamer, composed of four subunits, namely Cdc10, Cdc3, Cdc12 and Cdc11, arranged into two tetramers with two-fold rotational symmetry.
source: The basic structural unit of the yeast septin complex is an octamer, composed of four subunits, namely Cdc10, Cdc3, Cdc12 and Cdc11, arranged into two tetramers with two-fold rotational symmetry (Bertin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bertin et al., 2008.

claim: Cdc42 has been identified as a central regulator of septin ring assembly and disassembly during different stages of the cell cycle.
source: Cdc42 has been identified as a central regulator of septin ring assembly and disassembly during different stages of the cell cycle (Gladfelter et al., 2002; Kozminski et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gladfelter et al., 2002 and Kozminski et al., 2003.

claim: Mutations that affect the GTPase activity of Cdc42 impair the initial assembly of septin rings.
source: Mutations that affect the GTPase activity of Cdc42 impair the initial assembly of septin rings, while after bud emergence, septin rings are maintained independently of Ccd42 (Gladfelter et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gladfelter et al., 2002.

claim: After bud emergence, septin rings are maintained independently of Cdc42.
source: Mutations that affect the GTPase activity of Cdc42 impair the initial assembly of septin rings, while after bud emergence, septin rings are maintained independently of Ccd42 (Gladfelter et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gladfelter et al., 2002.

claim: The activity of Cdc42's guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and GTPase activating protein (GAP) are required for proper septin ring formation and localization.
source: It was also reported that the activity of Cdc42's guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and GTPase activating protein (GAP) are required for proper septin ring formation and localization, implying that one or more cycle(s) of nucleotide binding and hydrolysis are required for Cdc42 at the beginning of budding (Gladfelter et al., 2002; Caviston et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gladfelter et al., 2002 and Caviston et al., 2003.

claim: One or more cycle(s) of nucleotide binding and hydrolysis are required for Cdc42 at the beginning of budding.
source: It was also reported that the activity of Cdc42's guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and GTPase activating protein (GAP) are required for proper septin ring formation and localization, implying that one or more cycle(s) of nucleotide binding and hydrolysis are required for Cdc42 at the beginning of budding (Gladfelter et al., 2002; Caviston et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies (Gladfelter et al., 2002; Caviston et al., 2003).

claim: Gic1 and Gic2 are essential effectors of Cdc42 in yeast.
source: Among the essential effectors of Cdc42 in yeast are the two structurally homologous proteins Gic1 and Gic2, which are functional homologues of the human Borg protein (Joberty et al., 2001; Sheffield et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joberty et al., 2001 and Sheffield et al., 2003.

claim: Gic1 and Gic2 are structurally homologous proteins.
source: Among the essential effectors of Cdc42 in yeast are the two structurally homologous proteins Gic1 and Gic2, which are functional homologues of the human Borg protein (Joberty et al., 2001; Sheffield et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joberty et al., 2001 and Sheffield et al., 2003.

claim: Gic1 and Gic2 are functional homologues of the human Borg protein.
source: Among the essential effectors of Cdc42 in yeast are the two structurally homologous proteins Gic1 and Gic2, which are functional homologues of the human Borg protein (Joberty et al., 2001; Sheffield et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joberty et al., 2001 and Sheffield et al., 2003.

claim: Gic1 and Gic2 play an essential and overlapping role in cytoskeletal polarization.
source: It has been shown that Gic1 and Gic2 play an essential and overlapping role in cytoskeletal polarization (Brown et al., 1997; Hall and Russell, 2004) and septin recruitment (Iwase et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1997 and Hall and Russell, 2004.

claim: Gic1 and Gic2 play a role in septin recruitment.
source: It has been shown that Gic1 and Gic2 play an essential and overlapping role in cytoskeletal polarization (Brown et al., 1997; Hall and Russell, 2004) and septin recruitment (Iwase et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwase et al., 2006.

claim: EGFP-labeled septins without Gic1 form relatively short and straight filaments.
source: EGFP-labeled septins without Gic1 (Cdc3-EGFP, Cdc10, Cdc11 and Cdc12) form relatively short and straight filaments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When Gic1 is added during septin polymerization, long filaments that cluster together in large bundles are formed.
source: Interestingly, when Gic1 is added during septin polymerization, long filaments that cluster together in large bundles are formed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Blank septin polymers form long, often pairwise arranged filaments.
source: Studying the same but not EGFP-labeled samples using electron microscopy (EM), we found that in contrast to blank septin polymers that form long, often pairwise arranged filaments (Figure 1C), Gic1-septin complexes display a regular railroad-like structure with many cross-linked filaments bundled together (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gic1-septin complexes display a regular railroad-like structure with many cross-linked filaments bundled together.
source: Studying the same but not EGFP-labeled samples using electron microscopy (EM), we found that in contrast to blank septin polymers that form long, often pairwise arranged filaments (Figure 1C), Gic1-septin complexes display a regular railroad-like structure with many cross-linked filaments bundled together (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gic1 forms cross-bridges between at least two filaments, keeping them at a distance of about 20 nm.
source: Gic1 forms cross-bridges between at least two filaments, keeping them at a distance of about 20 nm (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM class averages shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At each cross-bridge, Gic1 binds to at least two adjacent septin subunits on each filament.
source: At each cross-bridge, Gic1 binds to at least two adjacent septin subunits on each filament (Figure 1F), leaving a gap of six free subunits between individual Gic1 molecules (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM class averages shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There is a gap of six free subunits between individual Gic1 molecules.
source: At each cross-bridge, Gic1 binds to at least two adjacent septin subunits on each filament (Figure 1F), leaving a gap of six free subunits between individual Gic1 molecules (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM class averages shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The structure of Gic1 is not well defined indicating that Gic1 is flexible and oriented differently at each cross-bridge.
source: The structure of Gic1 is not well defined (Figure 1F) indicating that Gic1 is flexible and oriented differently at each cross-bridge.
evidence: This is inferred from the EM class averages shown in Figure 1F where Gic1 density appears poorly defined.

claim: Cdc11 sits exactly in the middle of a septin filament between two Gic1 cross-bridges.
source: To determine which septin subunit interacts with Gic1, we labeled septin-Gic1 complexes with antibodies against Cdc11 and observed that it sits exactly in the middle of a septin filament between two Gic1 cross-bridges (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the antibody labeling EM data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Based on the known sequential order of septin filaments, Gic1 binds to Cdc10.
source: Based on the known sequential order of septin filaments, this suggests that Gic1 binds to Cdc10 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the antibody labeling data and the known septin arrangement from Bertin et al., 2008.

claim: Previous yeast two-hybrid, in vitro interaction and coimmunoprecipitation data indicated that Gic1 directly interacts with Cdc12.
source: However, previous yeast two-hybrid, in vitro interaction and coimmunoprecipitation data indicated that Gic1 directly interacts with Cdc12 (Iwase et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwase et al., 2006.

claim: Septin-Cdc10Δ, which formed short filaments, did not bind to Gic1.
source: As expected from the results of antibody labeling, septin-Cdc10Δ, which formed short filaments, did not bind to Gic1 (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Septin-Cdc11Δ does not polymerize.
source: Septin-Cdc11Δ, however, which in accordance with previous studies (Bertin et al., 2010) does not polymerize (Figure 2F) produced a similar track-like structure as the wildtype when Gic1 was added (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 2F and is consistent with previous studies cited (Bertin et al., 2010).

claim: Addition of Gic1 to septin-Cdc11Δ resulted in the binding of the protein to the septin complex and induced septin polymerization.
source: Thus, addition of Gic1 resulted not only in the binding of the protein to the septin complex but also induced septin polymerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the EM data shown in Figure 2G where septin-Cdc11Δ forms filaments in the presence of Gic1.

claim: Only four subunits were located between Gic1 cross-bridges of Cdc11Δ filaments, ruling out an interaction with Cdc12.
source: We then performed single particle analysis (SPA) of the septin filaments and observed that only four subunits were located between Gic1 cross-bridges of Cdc11Δ filaments, ruling out an interaction with Cdc12 (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the SPA class averages shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid studies showed that Gic1 only interacts with Cdc10.
source: In addition, yeast two-hybrid studies supported our in vitro data, showing that Gic1 only interacts with Cdc10 (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is directly observed in the yeast two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Cdc10 is mainly responsible for the specific interaction of septin filaments with PIP2, localizing them to membranes and promoting filament polymerization and organization.
source: Notably, Cdc10 is mainly responsible for the specific interaction of septin filaments with PIP2, localizing them to membranes and promoting filament polymerization and organization (Bertin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bertin et al., 2010.

claim: For Gic2, which is a homologue of Gic1, a direct interaction through its polybasic region with PIP2 was reported.
source: For Gic2, which is a homologue of Gic1, a direct interaction through its polybasic region with PIP2 was also reported (Orlando et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orlando et al., 2008.

claim: The organization and polymerization of septin filaments is controlled by the interaction of Gics with Cdc10 and the interaction of both proteins with PIP2.
source: Together with our findings, this suggests that the organization and polymerization of septin filaments is controlled by the interaction of Gics with Cdc10 and the interaction of both proteins with PIP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and the cited literature on PIP2 interactions.

claim: Septin filaments are cross-linked by overlapping C-terminal extensions of Cdc3 and Cdc12.
source: Bertin et al. reported that septin filaments are cross-linked by overlapping C-terminal extensions of Cdc3 and Cdc12 (Bertin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bertin et al., 2008.

claim: Gic1 simultaneously interacted with up to six septin polymers, forming long filament cables.
source: To study the native three-dimensional structure of the filaments, we vitrified septin-Gic1 complexes and determined their structure using cryo electron tomography (cryo-ET) (Figure 3; Videos 1–4). We observed that Gic1, instead of cross-bridging only two filaments, simultaneously interacted with up to six septin polymers, forming long filament cables (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-ET reconstructions shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Gic1 forms a central scaffold to which septin filaments attach.
source: The organization of these cables is such that Gic1 forms a central scaffold to which septin filaments attach.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-ET reconstructions shown in Figure 3.

claim: Individual septin filaments do not start at the same position and run along in parallel rigid lines.
source: Remarkably, individual septin filaments do not start at the same position and run along in parallel rigid lines.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-ET reconstructions shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: The septin-Gic1 cables are composed of many filaments of variable lengths that start at random positions, sometimes bypassing a Gic1 cross-bridge or changing place with another filament.
source: The septin-Gic1 cables are rather composed of many filaments of variable lengths that start at random positions, sometimes bypassing a Gic1 cross-bridge or changing place with another filament (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-ET reconstructions shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: Filaments are often only attached to adjacent filaments for several nanometers.
source: Filaments are often only attached to adjacent filaments for several nanometers.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-ET reconstructions shown in Figure 3.

claim: The flexibility of septin-Gic1 cables allows them to bend and adjust to membrane curvature.
source: This gives the septin-Gic1 cables a certain flexibility that on the one hand allows them to bend and adjust to membrane curvature (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The flexibility of septin-Gic1 cables enables the interaction between cables, resulting in mesh-like structures.
source: On the other hand it enables the interaction between cables, resulting in mesh-like structures (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Gic1(104-314) has a molecular weight of 23 kDa based on its sequence.
source: Gic1, which based on its sequence has a molecular weight of 23 kDa (Gic1(104-314)) (Figure 4A), elutes at about 49 kDa from a gel filtration column corresponding roughly to a dimer (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the protein sequence and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gic1(104-314) elutes at about 49 kDa from a gel filtration column corresponding roughly to a dimer.
source: Gic1, which based on its sequence has a molecular weight of 23 kDa (Gic1(104-314)) (Figure 4A), elutes at about 49 kDa from a gel filtration column corresponding roughly to a dimer (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the gel filtration data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In a typical Gic1 cross-bridge up to 12 Cdc10 subunits are involved (two per filament).
source: In a typical Gic1 cross-bridge up to 12 Cdc10 subunits are involved (two per filament) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-ET reconstructions shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The heterogeneity of the Gic1 cross-bridges suggests that the number of Gic1 molecules varies between cross-bridges.
source: In addition, the heterogeneity of the Gic1 cross-bridges suggests that the number of Gic1 molecules varies between cross-bridges.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed variability in Gic1 density in the EM and cryo-ET data.

claim: Gic1 and its homologue Gic2 are effectors of Cdc42, which bind via their CRIB motif to the GTP-bound form of the Rho GTPase in cells.
source: It was previously reported that Gic1 and its homologue Gic2 are effectors of Cdc42, which bind via their CRIB motif to the GTP-bound form of the Rho GTPase in cells (Brown et al., 1997; Chen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1997 and Chen et al., 1997.

claim: Gic1 formed a stable complex with Cdc42-GppNHp.
source: We made similar observations when studying the interaction of purified Gic1 and Cdc42 in vitro. Gic1 formed a stable complex with Cdc42-GppNHp (non-hydrolysable GTP analogue), but did not bind to Cdc42 in the GDP-state (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in the gel filtration data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Gic1 did not bind to Cdc42 in the GDP-state.
source: We made similar observations when studying the interaction of purified Gic1 and Cdc42 in vitro. Gic1 formed a stable complex with Cdc42-GppNHp (non-hydrolysable GTP analogue), but did not bind to Cdc42 in the GDP-state (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in the gel filtration data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Septin-Gic1 complexes produced in the presence of Cdc42-GppNHp have the same railroad-pattern as septin-Gic1 complexes, but with much bulkier cross-bridges.
source: On producing septin-Gic1 complexes in the presence of Cdc42-GppNHp, we found the same railroad-pattern as for the septin-Gic1 complexes, however, in this case with much bulkier cross-bridges (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The cross-bridges in septin-Gic1-Cdc42-GppNHp complexes were almost one and a half times larger in size, spanning not only two but four septin subunits, leaving only four septins unoccupied.
source: SPA and cryo-ET of the Gic1-Cdc42-septin complex revealed that the cross-bridges were almost one and a half times larger in size, spanning not only two but four septin subunits, leaving only four septins unoccupied (Figure 6B–I, Video 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in the SPA and cryo-ET data shown in Figure 6B-I.

claim: The larger cross-bridges in septin-Gic1-Cdc42-GppNHp complexes suggest a direct interaction of Cdc42-GppNHp with Gic1 on septin filaments.
source: This suggests a direct interaction of Cdc42-GppNHp with Gic1 on septin filaments (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing larger cross-bridges in the presence of Cdc42-GppNHp.

claim: An increase of the Cdc42-GppNHp concentration resulted in dissociation of the septin-Gic1-Cdc42 complex.
source: Unexpectedly, an increase of the Cdc42-GppNHp concentration resulted in dissociation of the septin-Gic1-Cdc42 complex (Figures 6D and 7).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figures 6D and 7.

claim: Full decoration of Gic1 with Cdc42 destabilizes the Gic1 interaction with septins, resulting in dissociation of the septin-Gic1-Cdc42 complex.
source: A possible explanation for this observation is that full decoration of Gic1 with Cdc42 destabilizes the Gic1 interaction with septins, resulting in dissociation of the septin-Gic1-Cdc42 complex.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed dissociation at high Cdc42-GppNHp concentrations.

claim: Cdc42-GDP did not bind to septin-Gic1 complexes even at 10 times higher concentrations.
source: In contrast, Cdc42-GDP did not bind to septin-Gic1 complexes even at 10 times higher concentrations (Figure 8).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Borg binds with its BD3 domain to SEPT7/SEPT6 dimers and induces the formation of long and thick septin filament fibers.
source: Similar behavior was reported for the functionally related human protein Borg (Joberty et al., 1999; Sirajuddin et al., 2007). Borg binds with its BD3 domain to SEPT7/SEPT6 dimers and induces the formation of long and thick septin filament fibers (Joberty et al., 2001; Sheffield et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joberty et al., 1999, 2001; Sirajuddin et al., 2007; Sheffield et al., 2003.

claim: Human Cdc42-GTP negatively regulates the Borg-septin association after binding to Borg.
source: In accordance with our observations with Cdc42-GTP, Gic1 and septin, the human Cdc42-GTP negatively regulates this process and after binding to Borg inhibits the Borg–septin association.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on Borg and compared to the authors' observations.

claim: Cdc42-GppNHp bound to septin filaments in the absence of Gic1, but no regular pattern was observed, indicating non-specific interaction.
source: To determine whether Cdc42 interacts directly with septins in the absence of Gic1, we produced septin filaments in the presence of Cdc42-GppHNp and Cdc42-GDP, respectively. Although Cdc42 in its GTP-state bound to septin filaments, no regular pattern as in the case of Gic1 was observed, indicating non-specific interaction (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Cdc42-GDP bound more specifically to septin filaments and formed railroad track-like structures.
source: Surprisingly, Cdc42-GDP bound more specifically to septin filaments, and formed, in contrast to Cdc42-GppNHp, railroad track-like structures (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Cdc42-GDP completely dissociated septin filaments at higher concentrations in less than an hour.
source: Even more surprising was that Cdc42-GDP completely dissociated septin filaments at higher concentrations in less than an hour (Figures 9C and 10).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figures 9C and 10.

claim: Cdc42-GDP binds to septin complexes as shown by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: We then analyzed the oligomers by size-exclusion chromatography, which showed that Cdc42-GDP binds to septin complexes (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the gel filtration data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: SPA of the dissociated septins identified either octamers with an extra density at their ends (90%) or hexamers without additional density (10%).
source: SPA of the dissociated septins clearly identified either octamers with an extra density at their ends (90%) or hexamers without additional density (10%) (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the SPA class averages shown in Figure 9E-F.

claim: Cdc42-GDP directly binds to Cdc10, thereby causing dissociation of the filaments.
source: Cdc3 sits at the ends of the hexamers, and at the second outer position of the octamers (Figure 9G–H). Considering the sequential order of septin oligomers, this indicates that Cdc42-GDP directly binds to Cdc10 (Figure 9I), which is also the binding partner of Gic1 (Figure 2), thereby causing dissociation of the filaments.
evidence: This is inferred from the antibody labeling data shown in Figure 9G-H and the known septin arrangement.

claim: The resulting septin octamers after Cdc42-GDP binding differ from the ones observed under high-salt conditions.
source: Consequently, the resulting septin octamers differ from the ones observed under high-salt conditions (Figure 11).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the structures shown in Figures 9 and 11.

claim: In septin octamers formed with Cdc42-GDP, Cdc11 is in the center instead of at the ends.
source: Instead of Cdc11, which is now in the center, Cdc10 forms the cap of the octamers at both ends.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of septin-Cdc42-GDP complexes.

claim: Binding of Cdc42-GDP to Cdc10 probably influences its interaction with Cdc3 at the G interface resulting in the formation of Cdc42-GDP-Cdc10 dimers and hexameric (Cdc3-Cdc12-Cdc11) complexes.
source: In addition, binding of Cdc42-GDP to Cdc10 probably influences its interaction with Cdc3 at the G interface resulting in the formation of Cdc42-GDP-Cdc10 dimers and hexameric (Cdc3-Cdc12-Cdc11) complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed hexamers and octamers.

claim: A direct interaction of a protein with Cdc42-GDP is unusual, since in most reported cases Cdc42, like other small G proteins, binds to its effectors in its active, that is GTP-bound state.
source: A direct interaction of a protein with Cdc42-GDP is unusual, since in most reported cases Cdc42, like other small G proteins, binds to its effectors in its active, that is GTP-bound state.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about small G proteins.

claim: Msb3 and Msb4, which are GAP proteins involved in cell polarization, were shown to directly interact with Cdc42-GDP.
source: However, also other proteins such as Msb3 and Msb4, which are GAP proteins, that are, like Gic1, involved in cell polarization, were shown to directly interact with Cdc42-GDP (Tcheperegine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tcheperegine et al., 2005.

claim: The N-terminal region of Cdc10 is the least conserved among the four septin structures.
source: To identify the Cdc42 binding site on Cdc10, we calculated homology models of Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11 and Cdc12 using the SEPT2 structure (PDB 2QA5) as a reference and mapped regions of conservation between the four structures on their surfaces. Examining the Cdc10-Cdc10 interface, which is an N/C interface, we found that the N-terminal region is the least conserved, and would therefore present an ideal site for specific Cdc42-GDP binding (Figure 12A–B).
evidence: This is inferred from the homology modeling and conservation analysis shown in Figure 12.

claim: The N-terminal region of Cdc10 would present an ideal site for specific Cdc42-GDP binding.
source: Examining the Cdc10-Cdc10 interface, which is an N/C interface, we found that the N-terminal region is the least conserved, and would therefore present an ideal site for specific Cdc42-GDP binding (Figure 12A–B).
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation analysis shown in Figure 12.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal 29 residues of Cdc10 results in non-polymerizing septin complexes forming tetramers and inside-out octamers.
source: We deleted the N-terminal 29 residues of Cdc10 and produced complexes whose Cdc10 was replaced by Cdc10(30-322). It was previously shown that deletion of the N-terminal residues of Cdc10 results in non-polymerizing septin complexes forming tetramers and inside-out octamers (Bertin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bertin et al., 2010.

claim: Most of the septin-Cdc10(30-322) complexes were tetramers or octamers, and the polymerization of the complexes was clearly impaired.
source: We analyzed the particles by EM and SPA, which showed that most of the complexes were indeed tetramers or octamers, and that the polymerization of the complexes was clearly impaired, as we did not observe filaments at low-salt conditions (Figure 13A–C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM and SPA data shown in Figure 13A-C.

claim: Cdc42-GDP does not bind to Cdc10(30-322).
source: We then incubated the oligomers with high concentrations of Cdc42-GDP and looked for additional densities corresponding to Cdc42-GDP by EM and SPA. However, no additional protein was bound to the tetramers or octamers (Figure 13D–F). Gel filtration experiments corroborated this result and showed that indeed Cdc42-GDP does not bind to Cdc10(30-322) (Figure 13G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM, SPA, and gel filtration data shown in Figure 13D-G.

claim: The N-terminal region of Cdc10 is essential for the binding of Cdc42-GDP to septin filaments.
source: This indicates that the N-terminal region of Cdc10 is essential for the binding of Cdc42-GDP to septin filaments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Cdc42-GDP does not bind to Cdc10(30-322).

claim: The N-terminal region of Cdc10 was shown to be important for the interaction of septin filaments with PIP2.
source: Interestingly, the same region on Cdc10 was shown to be important for the interaction of septin filaments with PIP2 (Bertin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bertin et al., 2010.

claim: In septin-Gic1 complexes Cdc42-GDP binds neither to septins nor to Gic1.
source: From our previous experiments, we know that in septin-Gic1 complexes Cdc42-GDP binds neither to septins nor to Gic1 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Both Gic1 and Cdc42-GDP bind to Cdc10 and very probably compete for the same binding site.
source: Since both Gic1 and Cdc42-GDP bind to Cdc10 and very probably compete for the same binding site, Gic1 must have a higher affinity for Cdc10 than Cdc42-GDP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations that both proteins bind Cdc10 and that Gic1 can displace Cdc42-GDP.

claim: Gic1 must have a higher affinity for Cdc10 than Cdc42-GDP.
source: Since both Gic1 and Cdc42-GDP bind to Cdc10 and very probably compete for the same binding site, Gic1 must have a higher affinity for Cdc10 than Cdc42-GDP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Gic1 can displace Cdc42-GDP from septin complexes.

claim: Gic1 replaced Cdc42-GDP to interact with Cdc10, resulting in septin polymerization when added to septin-Cdc42-GDP complexes.
source: In order to prove this, we added Gic1 to septin-Cdc42-GDP complexes (Figure 14A–B). As expected, we found long railroad track-like ordered filaments indicating that Gic1 replaced Cdc42-GDP to interact with Cdc10, resulting in septin polymerization.
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 14A-B.

claim: Septin-Gic1 filament complexes were observed when Gic1 was mixed with octamers under high-salt conditions that normally inhibit polymerization.
source: We also observed septin-Gic1 filament complexes when we mixed Gic1 with octamers under conditions that normally inhibit polymerization, such as high-salt buffer (Figure 14C–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 14C-D.

claim: The stabilizing effect of Gic1 must be stronger than the weakening effect of high salt on septin filaments.
source: This was surprising, since Gic1 binds and crosslinks Cdc10 proteins while high salt weakens the interaction at the N/C-interface between two Cdc11 proteins. Thus, the stabilizing effect of Gic1 must be stronger than the weakening effect of high salt.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that septin-Gic1 complexes form even under high-salt conditions.

claim: Septin-Gic1 complexes were stable and did not dissociate when dialyzed against a high-salt buffer.
source: We confirmed this observation by performing the inverse experiment, that is septin-Gic1 complexes were dialyzed against a high-salt buffer. As expected, septin-Gic1 complexes were stable and did not dissociate (Figure 14E–F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 14E-F.

claim: Septin complexes completely lacking Cdc11 do not polymerize at low-salt conditions, but form filaments when Gic1 is added.
source: Even septin complexes completely lacking Cdc11, which do not polymerize at low-salt conditions, form filaments when Gic1 is added (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Gic1 not only scaffolds septin filaments, but also increases their stability.
source: Taken together, we conclude that Gic1 not only scaffolds septin filaments, but also increases their stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that Gic1 stabilizes filaments under high-salt conditions and induces polymerization of Cdc11Δ septins.

claim: Gic1 did not induce filament formation of septin-Cdc10(30-322) complexes.
source: We then asked whether Gic1 would also stabilize septin filaments whose assembly is weakened at the Cdc10-Cdc10 instead of the Cdc11-Cdc11 interface. As shown above, complexes whose Cdc10 is replaced by Cdc10(30-322) do not polymerize at all and form tetramers or inside-out octamers (Figure 13A–C). Interestingly, Gic1 did not induce filament formation of such impaired septins (Figure 13H), but still bound to Cdc10(30-322) as indicated by an additional density attached to the septin oligomers and by size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 13I–L).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM and gel filtration data shown in Figure 13H-L.

claim: Gic1 still bound to Cdc10(30-322) as indicated by an additional density attached to the septin oligomers and by size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Interestingly, Gic1 did not induce filament formation of such impaired septins (Figure 13H), but still bound to Cdc10(30-322) as indicated by an additional density attached to the septin oligomers and by size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 13I–L).
evidence: This is directly observed in the EM and gel filtration data shown in Figure 13I-L.

claim: Cdc42-GDP recruits septin octamers (with Cdc10 at the caps) to the bud site.
source: Because Cdc42-GDP binds to Cdc10 in septin complexes and prevents their polymerization, we propose that Cdc42-GDP rather than Gic1 recruits septin octamers (with Cdc10 at the caps) to the bud site (Figure 16A).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: At the bud site Cdc42 interacts with its GEF Cdc24, which catalyzes the exchange of its nucleotide.
source: At the bud site Cdc42 interacts with its GEF Cdc24, which catalyzes the exchange of its nucleotide (Figure 16B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism and is based on established knowledge about Cdc42 and Cdc24.

claim: As a result of nucleotide exchange, Cdc42 dissociates from the septin complexes, which in turn polymerize.
source: As a result, Cdc42 dissociates from the septin complexes, which in turn polymerize.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cdc42-GTP recruits its effector Gic1 to the bud site.
source: Besides activating many other proteins involved in septin recruitment and ring formation Cdc42-GTP recruits its effector Gic1 to the bud site (Figure 16C).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism and is consistent with known Cdc42-Gic1 interactions.

claim: Gic1 binds, scaffolds and stabilizes septin filaments at the bud site.
source: Gic1, which has a high affinity for Cdc10, binds, scaffolds and stabilizes septin filaments (Figure 16D).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Gic1-Cdc42-GTP-septin cables form a ring at the bud neck.
source: Gic1-Cdc42-GTP-septin cables generated in this manner form a ring at the bud neck.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The process of Gic1-septin cable formation does not necessarily require Cdc42-GTP.
source: Since our data show that the process of Gic1-septin cable formation does not necessarily require Cdc42-GTP, we propose that upon GAP-supported GTP hydrolysis, Cdc42-GDP, which has a much lower affinity to Gic1 than Cdc42-GTP, dissociates from the Gic1-septin complex (Figure 16E) and recruits more septin octamers to the bud site (Figure 16F).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Gic1 can form complexes with septins in the absence of Cdc42-GTP.

claim: Upon GAP-supported GTP hydrolysis, Cdc42-GDP dissociates from the Gic1-septin complex.
source: Since our data show that the process of Gic1-septin cable formation does not necessarily require Cdc42-GTP, we propose that upon GAP-supported GTP hydrolysis, Cdc42-GDP, which has a much lower affinity to Gic1 than Cdc42-GTP, dissociates from the Gic1-septin complex (Figure 16E) and recruits more septin octamers to the bud site (Figure 16F).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: At later stages of the cell cycle the local Cdc42-GTP concentration increases at the bud neck, probably caused by an up-regulation of Cdc24 and/or identical spatial localization.
source: At later stages of the cell cycle the local Cdc42-GTP concentration increases at the bud neck, probably caused by an up-regulation of Cdc24 and/or identical spatial localization (Butty et al., 2002; Goryachev and Pokhilko, 2008).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism and is supported by citations to Butty et al., 2002 and Goryachev and Pokhilko, 2008.

claim: Cdc42-GTP binds to Gic1-septin complexes and competes with Cdc10 for Gic1, which results in the disassembly of the complex and septin ring rearrangement.
source: As a result, Cdc42-GTP binds to Gic1-septin complexes and competes with Cdc10 for Gic1, which finally results in the disassembly of the complex and thereby septin ring rearrangement (Figure 16G).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: After GTP hydrolysis, Cdc42-GDP in the absence of Gic1 specifically binds to septin filaments and dissociates them.
source: After GTP hydrolysis, Cdc42-GDP in the absence of Gic1 specifically binds to septin filaments and dissociates them (Figure 16H).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Septins can be reassembled and reused for the next cycle, as was observed by McMurray and Thorner when tracking labeled septins through several cell divisions.
source: Thus, septins can be reassembled and reused for the next cycle, as was observed by McMurray and Thorner when tracking labeled septins through several cell divisions (McMurray and Thorner, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMurray and Thorner, 2009.

claim: The model elegantly explains the cycles of GTP loading and hydrolysis by Cdc42 that were observed by Gladfelter et al. during budding.
source: The model elegantly explains the cycles of GTP loading and hydrolysis by Cdc42 that were observed by Gladfelter et al. during budding (Gladfelter et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the proposed model fits with previous observations cited (Gladfelter et al., 2002).

claim: Gic1 and Cdc42 in combination with many other factors regulate septin recruitment, ring formation and disassembly.
source: In conclusion, Gic1 and Cdc42 in combination with many other factors, such as the nucleotide state of septins, specific interaction with lipids and protein posttranslational modifications regulate septin recruitment, ring formation and disassembly.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings and the proposed model.

claim: Cdc42 does not only act as a regulator, but seems to be also involved in septin recruitment.
source: Most importantly, Cdc42 does not only act as a regulator, but seems to be also involved in septin recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing Cdc42-GDP binding to septins.
